```markdown
# Batch Tracking: Mash Day to Bottle

## Intent
The brewery needs to trace any bottle back to the ingredients that went
into it. A bottle in a customer's hand leads to its batch, and the batch
leads to the lot number of every malt and hop sack used in it. This
matters for recalls, supplier quality problems, and answering "what's in
this bottle" with certainty instead of memory.

## Goals
- Record each batch from mash day through bottling.
- Record every malt and hop sack opened for a batch, by its supplier lot
  number.
- Print bottle labels carrying the batch number and bottling date.
- Trace in both directions: bottle → batch → sack lots, and
  sack lot → every batch that used it (for a supplier recall).

## Non-goals
- Inventory, stock levels, or reordering.
- Recipe management or brewing calculations.
- Costing or links to the taproom tabs.
- Tracing to individual bottles. Tracing works at the batch level.

## Anti-goals (failure even if it technically works)
- Brewers have to type lot numbers with wet hands. Scanning is the
  default path.
- Recording a sack takes long enough that people skip it on a busy
  mash day. One scan per sack, no extra screens.
- A batch can be bottled with gaps in its record and nobody notices.

## Constraints
- Runs on the existing Raspberry Pi in the office, alongside the
  taproom Flask app, using the same SQLite database.
- Usable in the brewhouse by brewers whose hands are usually wet.
- Uses the existing label printer for bottling runs.

## Approaches considered
1. **Extend the existing Flask app with a batch-tracking module.**
   (chosen) Same Pi, same database, same deployment, nothing new to run
   or back up. The cost is that the taproom app and batch tracking share
   one process, so a bug in one can take down the other.
2. **A separate small app on the same Pi.** Keeps them apart, but means
   a second service, second database, and second backup for a small
   brewery with one machine. The isolation isn't worth that here.
3. **A spreadsheet or off-the-shelf brewery software.** A spreadsheet
   can't drive scanning or the label printer cleanly. Hosted brewery
   software adds a subscription and an internet dependency, and doesn't
   use the setup already in place.

Approach 1 was my call; the partner handed over how it's built.

## What was agreed in conversation
- A batch is the unit of tracing. Each one has a batch number.
- Malt and hop sacks carry supplier lot numbers.
- A sack's lot number is **scanned when the sack is opened**, not typed,
  because brewers' hands are usually wet.
- At bottling, each label gets the batch number and the bottling date.
- Bottle → batch → every sack lot is the chain that must hold.

## Design
Units, each with one purpose:

- **Data (SQLite tables)**
  - `batches`: batch number, beer name, mash date, status
    (brewing / bottled), bottling date.
  - `sack_uses`: batch, ingredient type (malt / hop), supplier lot
    number, time scanned.
  - `bottling_runs`: batch, bottling date, label count printed.
- **Brewhouse screen**: open batch, show sacks scanned so far, one
  input that accepts a scan and records it immediately. Large text and
  buttons for use at a distance and with wet hands.
- **Bottling screen**: pick the batch, confirm the sack list, set the
  label count, print. Marks the batch bottled.
- **Label printing**: one small module that turns batch number and
  bottling date into the printer's format and sends it.
- **Trace screen**: enter a batch number (from a bottle) to see its sack
  lots; enter a lot number to see every batch that used it.

## My calls (correct any of these)
- Scanning by a USB or Bluetooth barcode scanner acting as a keyboard,
  into a browser page served by the Pi. No camera scanning, no app
  install.
- Batch numbers generated by the system in sequence, e.g. `B-2026-041`.
- A scanned lot can be removed from a batch before bottling (mis-scan),
  but not after.

## Left to the builder
- Table and route names, following the existing app's patterns.
- Label layout within the printer's size limits.
- How the brewhouse screen shows a successful scan (sound, color).
```

I'm writing it up now. You handed me how it gets built, so here are my calls:

- **Build approach:** I'm adding this as a new part of the taproom app on the same Pi and database, not as a separate system or a spreadsheet. That means nothing new to run or back up.
- **Scanning:** a cheap barcode scanner plugged into a tablet or laptop in the brewhouse. It fills in a browser page served by the Pi, so nothing needs installing.

A reviewer is reading the draft first, as if they had to build from it alone. I may come back once with a few questions only you can answer. After that, I'll give you the finished document and a short list of the other calls I made so you can check them.

One heads-up: this folder isn't under git yet. When I hand the document over I'll set that up so the design is saved properly, unless you'd rather I didn't.
